theme: Unit 25 review, The New Covenant Consummated, Revelation
memoryText: Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This is the memory verse for the final unit, and the destination of the whole Bible. Notice how it begins: “Behold.” It is a call to look. After all of history, John is told to look at what God has done.

“The dwelling place of God is with man.” The Hebrew Scriptures speak of God’s tabernacle, the glory in the temple, and the promise “I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” The story began in a garden, where God walked with Adam and Eve. Sin separated us. Christ came, “and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). And now God dwells with us forever.

Then the promise: “He will wipe away every tear.” God personally wipes tears. It is the picture of a tender Father. “Death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.” Every grief that you carry will be answered.

Say this verse to yourself in the hardest moments, and say it to someone who is grieving. It is not wishful thinking. It is a promise from the one who said, “Behold, I am making all things new.”
unitRecap: This final unit took us through the book of Revelation, in which all of God’s covenant promises find their Yes in Christ. In chapters 1 to 3, we saw the risen Christ among his churches, and his letters calling them to love, faithfulness, and repentance. In chapters 4 and 5, we entered the throne room, where the Lion of Judah is a Lamb who was slain, worthy to open the scroll of history. The seals, trumpets, and bowls showed God’s judgment on a rebellious world and the church’s call to endure, with the sealed multitude from every nation. Chapters 12 and 13 unmasked the dragon and the beasts, and showed that the saints conquer by the blood of the Lamb, by the word of their testimony, and by not loving their lives even unto death. Chapters 17 to 20 showed the fall of Babylon, the marriage supper of the Lamb, Christ’s return, the defeat of Satan, and the final judgment. Chapters 21 and 22 revealed the new heavens and new earth, with God dwelling with his people, the river and tree of life, and the final invitation, “Come.” Psalms 1, 19, 29, 141, 150, 148, 2, 46, 93, 97, and 72 provided songs along the way: the two ways, creation and word, the voice of the LORD, prayers as incense, praise, and the reign of God. The doctrinal pauses covered the final judgment and the new creation.

reviewQuestions.question: How does Revelation draw on imagery from every major section of the Old Testament?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Choose two images from Revelation (for example, the tree of life, the plagues, or the temple) and trace where they come from in the Old Testament.

reviewQuestions.question: What does it mean that the Lamb who was slain holds the scroll of history?
reviewQuestions.prompt: In your own words, explain how Christ’s death is the key to history, and how this might change the way you see current events.

reviewQuestions.question: How do Revelation 21 and 22 fulfill the promises of Genesis 1 and 2?
reviewQuestions.prompt: List three things from the Garden of Eden that return in the new creation, and say what each tells you about God’s purpose.

reviewQuestions.question: Looking back: where do you see God’s covenant faithfulness from beginning to end?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Name three moments in the Bible’s story where God kept his promises, and one moment in your own life where you have seen his faithfulness.

prayerPrompts: Thank God that he will dwell with you and wipe away every tear.
Tell him what you have seen of the Lamb in Revelation.
Ask him to keep the unit verse before you.
